# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic — **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout — so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* …only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above — the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(…)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
|

tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).

## Surfaces (for the validator)

- Light chart surface: `#fcfcfb`

These are the validator's built-in defaults. **When you swap in your own

## Chart chrome & ink

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| Chart surface | `#fcfcfb` | `#1a1a19` |

## Filter controls

Filters are standard UI, not chart components — the chart layer only adds the
composition rules in `interaction.md`. A date-range control is a list of preset
rows (today, last 7/30/90 days, month-to-date) with selection marked by a 16px
bold check, hover as a ghost wash, and custom range behind a hairline in the
footer. Dimension filters are a standard combobox.

Everything — including the hero figure — stays in the system sans: `system-ui,

teColumns()`, `inferPrimaryKey()` |\n\n**Deliberate simplifications**, made because this is a demo tool for\ndatasets that fit comfortably in a browser tab, not a scale target:\n\n- No sampling for schema inference on undeclared tables — the JS engine just\n  looks at every row, because in-browser datasets are small enough that doing\n  so costs nothing. (`pipeline_spark/` samples specifically because *its*\n  datasets might not be.)\n- The \"conflicting duplicate key\" detail pandas surfaces\n  (`groupby(key).nunique()` — do the duplicate rows actually disagree on any\n  field) isn't separately reported here; a duplicate key is just a duplicate\n  key. It still reaches final QC as a hard failure if it survives filtering,\n  same as the Python version.\n- No file-size guard beyond what a browser tab can hold. `data/`'s ~30K-row\n  dataset runs in well under a second; a truly huge dataset belongs in\n  `pipeline_spark/`, not a browser tab.\n\n## Design notes\n\nPalette and type choices are documented as CSS custom properties at the top\nof `index.html` (`:root`, plus the two dark-mode blocks) — an \"inspection\nline\" visual language (manifest cards, severity badges, a schematic of the\npipeline as literal stages-in-sequence) rather than a generic dashboard\ntemplate. ### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T04:53:22.169Z</sub>

Live here (private — share it from the page's share menu when you want others to see it): **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1e6d0dc2-cd05-4a0d-b0d1-5b61b4ddc970**

Built on a new branch **`pipeline-visualizer-webapp`** (off the bigdata branch), pushed to origin.

**What it is** — a single self-contained page, no server, no build step. Upload CSVs (or click one of three embedded sample buttons), hit **Run pipeline**, and watch a live schematic animate through all seven stages while a manifest panel unfurls each stage's actual findings — row counts, QC issues color-coded by severity, filter log, then the revenue report with a segment bar chart and top-5 table.

**It's not a mockup** — I ported the pipeline logic to JavaScript and verified it against your real data before publishing: same total revenue ($16,153,512.87), same net revenue, same QC findings, to the cent. I also caught and fixed a real gap while testing — the JS wasn't yet honoring the Python pipeline's `raise_if_failed()` gate, so a hard QC failure was still showing a "trustworthy" report. Now a hard failure shows **BLOCKED** and withholds the numbers, exactly like the CLI would.

**Test datasets** (`webapp/sample_data/`), each verified through the engine before committing:
- `clean_batch/` — everything passes
- `dirty_batch/` — duplicates, an orphaned customer, a bad date, negative/zero amounts, an oversized discount, **plus a conflicting duplicate order_id that deliberately halts the pipeline** — the one sample built specifically to demonstrate that path
- `generalization_batch/` — a `returns.csv` the pipeline has no schema for, still profiled and cleaned generically
- for a real-scale test, upload the actual take-home data at `data/` in the repo

`webapp/README.md` explains the architecture, a function-by-function map back to `pipeline/*.py`, and what's deliberately simplified for a browser demo. Color palette (segment chart + severity badges) was chosen and validated for colorblind-safe separation, not eyeballed.

1	# Pipeline Inspector — a visual front end for the data-quality pipeline
2	
3	A single self-contained web page (`index.html`) that runs the same seven-stage
4	pipeline as `pipeline/` — ingest → QC (raw) → filter → clean → transform →
5	QC (final) → results — live, in the browser, on whatever CSVs you upload.
6	Nothing is sent anywhere: parsing, validation, and the revenue calculation all
7	happen client-side in JavaScript. There is no server and no build step —
8	open the file and it works.
9	
10	## Using it
11	
12	1. Open `index.html` in a browser (double-click it, or `open webapp/index.html`).
13	2. Provide a dataset, either:
14	   - drag/drop or browse to `.csv` files, or
15	   - click one of the three **sample** buttons for an instant demo
16	     (small datasets embedded directly in the page — see "Samples", below).
17	3. Click **Run pipeline**. The diagram animates stage by stage; a manifest
18	   card unfolds under each stage as it completes, and the final report
19	   (or an explanation of why there isn't one) appears at the bottom.
20	4. **Download QC report (.json)** / **Download results (.json)** save exactly
21	   what the equivalent Python run would have written to `pipeline_output/`.
22	
23	Tables are matched by filename: `customers.csv` / `orders.csv` /
24	`promotions.csv` get the exact, declared-schema treatment (typed columns,
25	required-column checks, the revenue join); anything else is still ingested,
26	profiled, filtered, and cleaned, using the same sample-free-because-it's-all-
27	in-memory version of the inference `pipeline/introspect.py` uses for
28	undeclared tables — see "How this maps to the Python pipeline," below.
29	
30	## Samples
31	
32	Three quick-demo buttons load small datasets **embedded directly in the
33	page** (no download needed):
34	
35	| Button | What it shows |
36	|---|---|
37	| Clean batch | A well-formed dataset — every stage completes with no findings. |
38	| Dirty batch | A handful of common issues (duplicate row, unex

... [3,722 characters omitted] ...

demo tool for
87	datasets that fit comfortably in a browser tab, not a scale target:
88	
89	- No sampling for schema inference on undeclared tables — the JS engine just
90	  looks at every row, because in-browser datasets are small enough that doing
91	  so costs nothing. (`pipeline_spark/` samples specifically because *its*
92	  datasets might not be.)
93	- The "conflicting duplicate key" detail pandas surfaces
94	  (`groupby(key).nunique()` — do the duplicate rows actually disagree on any
95	  field) isn't separately reported here; a duplicate key is just a duplicate
96	  key. It still reaches final QC as a hard failure if it survives filtering,
97	  same as the Python version.
98	- No file-size guard beyond what a browser tab can hold. `data/`'s ~30K-row
99	  dataset runs in well under a second; a truly huge dataset belongs in
100	  `pipeline_spark/`, not a browser tab.
101	
102	## Design notes
103	
104	Palette and type choices are documented as CSS custom properties at the top
105	of `index.html` (`:root`, plus the two dark-mode blocks) — an "inspection
106	line" visual language (manifest cards, severity badges, a schematic of the
107	pipeline as literal stages-in-sequence) rather than a generic dashboard
108	template. The categorical chart palette (revenue-by-segment) and the four
109	status colors (fail/warn/info/pass) were chosen and checked for
110	colorblind-safe separation using the validator in Anthropic's `dataviz`
111	skill; segment colors are assigned by name, not by sort order, so a
112	segment's color never changes depending on which one happens to lead that run.
113	
114	## Files
115	
116	```
117	index.html            the entire app — HTML, CSS, and JS, self-contained
118	sample_data/
119	  clean_batch/         customers.csv, orders.csv, promotions.csv
120	  dirty_batch/         same three, deliberately dirty (see table above)
121	  generalization_batch/  clean data + returns.csv, an undeclared table
122	README.md              this file
123	```
124

  "new_string": "## What's in the Report section\n\nEvery run — clean, dirty, blocked, or missing a table — shows all three of\nthese, in order, before anything specific to whether there's a revenue\nnumber to report:\n\n**Data health.** A single status pill — `Healthy`, `Clean, with notes`,\n`Needs review`, or `Blocked` — plus three concrete numbers: the fail/warn/info\nissue count across *both* QC passes combined, what percentage of the primary\ntable's rows (`orders`, if present) survived from ingestion through to the\nfinal table, and how many rows filtering dropped. The status is derived\ndirectly from issue severity (any `fail` → Blocked; any `warn` → Needs review;\nonly `info` → Clean, with notes; nothing → Healthy) — it's not a fabricated\nscore, just a direct readout of what the two QC passes already found.\n\n**QC comparison — before vs after.** A small counts table (fail/warn/info,\ninitial vs final) followed by the two full issue lists side by side: what\nStage 2 found in the raw data, and what Stage 6 found in the pipeline's own\noutput afterward. Reading them together shows what filtering/cleaning/\ntransform actually resolved (e.g. exact duplicates — gone by Stage 6) versus\nwhat only got labeled and passed through (e.g. an unknown customer — still\ncounted, just tagged `Unknown`, forever).\n\n**What the pipeline changed.** Three short, data-derived lists — Filtering,\nCleaning, Transform — written in plain language from the actual run, not\ntemplated text: which filter rules dropped rows and how many, what got\ntype-cast or collapsed during cleaning (including exactly how many\npromotion rows collapsed into how many order-level rows), and — if the\nrevenue transform ran — how many orders referenced an unknown customer and\nhow many discounts got capped, with the dollar amount.\n\nThese three are why the QC report download (below) is worth opening even on\na run that produced a full, boring, healthy report: it's the same \"what\nactually happened to my data\" narrative, saved to a file.\n\n## What \"blocked\" means"

1	# Pipeline Inspector — a visual front end for the data-quality pipeline
2	
3	A single self-contained web page (`index.html`) that runs the same seven-stage
4	pipeline as `pipeline/` — ingest → QC (raw) → filter → clean → transform →
5	QC (final) → results — live, in the browser, on whatever CSVs you upload.
6	Nothing is sent anywhere: parsing, validation, and the revenue calculation all
7	happen client-side in JavaScript. There is no server and no build step —
8	open the file and it works.
9	
10	## Using it
11	
12	1. Open `index.html` in a browser (double-click it, or `open webapp/index.html`).
13	2. Provide a dataset, either:
14	   - drag/drop or browse to `.csv` files, or
15	   - click one of the three **sample** buttons for an instant demo
16	     (small datasets embedded directly in the page — see "Samples", below).
17	3. Click **Run pipeline**. The diagram animates stage by stage; a manifest
18	   card unfolds under each stage as it completes. Below that, the Report
19	   section always shows three things regardless of what you uploaded — a
20	   **data health** summary, a **before/after QC comparison**, and a plain-
21	   language account of **what filtering, cleaning, and the join actually did**
22	   — and then either the revenue dashboard, a note that revenue needs all
23	   three known tables, or a **blocked** notice (see below).
24	4. **Download QC report (.md / .json)** save all of the above — health,
25	   comparison, change summary, and results if there are any — in one file,
26	   readable or machine-parseable.
27	
28	Tables are matched by filename: `customers.csv` / `orders.csv` /
29	`promotions.csv` get the exact, declared-schema treatment (typed columns,
30	required-column checks, the revenue join); anything else is still ingested,
31	profiled, filtered, and cleaned, using the same sample-free-because-it's-all-
32	in-memory version of the inference `pipeline/introspect.py` uses for
33	undeclared tables — see "How this maps to the Python pipeline,

... [6,533 characters omitted] ...


132	datasets that fit comfortably in a browser tab, not a scale target:
133	
134	- No sampling for schema inference on undeclared tables — the JS engine just
135	  looks at every row, because in-browser datasets are small enough that doing
136	  so costs nothing. (`pipeline_spark/` samples specifically because *its*
137	  datasets might not be.)
138	- The "conflicting duplicate key" detail pandas surfaces
139	  (`groupby(key).nunique()` — do the duplicate rows actually disagree on any
140	  field) isn't separately reported here; a duplicate key is just a duplicate
141	  key. It still reaches final QC as a hard failure if it survives filtering,
142	  same as the Python version.
143	- No file-size guard beyond what a browser tab can hold. `data/`'s ~30K-row
144	  dataset runs in well under a second; a truly huge dataset belongs in
145	  `pipeline_spark/`, not a browser tab.
146	
147	## Design notes
148	
149	Palette and type choices are documented as CSS custom properties at the top
150	of `index.html` (`:root`, plus the two dark-mode blocks) — an "inspection
151	line" visual language (manifest cards, severity badges, a schematic of the
152	pipeline as literal stages-in-sequence) rather than a generic dashboard
153	template. The categorical chart palette (revenue-by-segment) and the four
154	status colors (fail/warn/info/pass) were chosen and checked for
155	colorblind-safe separation using the validator in Anthropic's `dataviz`
156	skill; segment colors are assigned by name, not by sort order, so a
157	segment's color never changes depending on which one happens to lead that run.
158

165	  dirty_batch/         same three, deliberately dirty (see table above)
166	  generalization_batch/  clean data + returns.csv, an undeclared table
167	README.md              this file

### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T05:12:32.561Z</sub>

Same link, updated: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1e6d0dc2-cd05-4a0d-b0d1-5b61b4ddc970**

Every run now shows, always, before any revenue numbers:

- **Data health** — a status pill (Healthy / Clean with notes / Needs review / Blocked) derived directly from issue severity, plus row-retention % and rows-dropped-by-filtering. No fabricated score — just a direct readout of what the two QC passes found.
- **QC comparison — before vs after** — a fail/warn/info counts table plus the full initial-QC (raw data) and final-QC (pipeline output) issue lists side by side, so it's visible at a glance what got resolved (exact duplicates, gone by Stage 6) versus what only got labeled and carried through (an unknown customer, still `Unknown` forever).
- **What the pipeline changed** — plain-language, data-derived summaries of filtering (which rules dropped how many rows), cleaning (type coercions, promo-aggregation counts), and transform (unknown-customer count, discount-capping count and dollar amount).

These three render even on a **blocked** run — they describe what happened, which is true regardless of whether the revenue number is trustworthy; only the dashboard itself withholds numbers when blocked. The two download buttons now produce one comprehensive report (Markdown for reading, JSON for parsing) containing all of the above, always available once a run has happened.

While building the test harness to verify this against real output rather than just re-reading the code, I caught a real bug in my own test data: `generalization_batch/returns.csv` had two rows meant to be an exact duplicate, but they differed in their own ID column — so nothing actually caught them. Fixed and re-verified all four datasets (the real 30K-row data plus all three sample batches) produce the correct health status and exact same revenue numbers as before.

1	# Pipeline Inspector — a visual front end for the data-quality pipeline
2	
3	A single self-contained web page (`index.html`) that runs the same seven-stage

5	QC (final) → results — live, in the browser, on whatever CSVs you upload.
6	Nothing is sent anywhere: parsing, validation, and the revenue calculation all
7	happen client-side in JavaScript. There is no server and no build step —
8	open the file and it works.

10	## Using it
11	
12	1. Open `index.html` in a browser (double-click it, or `open webapp/index.html`).
13	2. Provide a dataset, either:
14	   - drag/drop or browse to `.csv` files, or
15	   - click one of the three **sample** buttons for an instant demo
16	     (small datasets embedded directly in the page — see "Samples", below).

18	   card unfolds under each stage as it completes. Below that, the Report
19	   section always shows three things regardless of what you uploaded — a
20	   **data health** summary, a **before/after QC comparison**, and a plain-
21	   language account of **what filtering, cleaning, and the join actually did**
22	   — and then either the revenue dashboard, a note that revenue needs all
23	   three known tables, or a **blocked** notice (see below).
24	4. **Download QC report (.md / .json)** save all of the above — health,
25	   comparison, change summary, and results if there are any — in one file,
26	   readable or machine-parseable.
27

99	## What "blocked" means
100	
101	The Python pipeline's `run.py` calls `final_qc.raise_if_failed()` before
102	writing any output — a hard (`fail`-severity) finding in the final QC stage
103	means the run stops and nothing gets written, on the theory that a report
104	built on data that failed its own validation isn't worth trusting just
105	because it happens to compute. This page mirrors that: if the final QC stage
106	finds a hard failure, Stage 7 shows **BLOCKED**, and the revenue dashboard —
107	stat tiles, segment chart, top-5 table — is replaced with a note explaining
108	why, instead of numbers computed from an unvalidated table. The data health,
109	QC comparison, and change summary above it are unaffected and still fully
110	populated (and still downloadable) — they describe what happened during the
111	run, which is true and useful information regardless of whether the final
112	number is trustworthy. The `dirty_batch/` sample above is built specifically
113	to demonstrate this path — everything else in the repo's sample data produces
114	a full report.
115	
```

A print stylesheet hides everything else on\nthe page and forces light, high-contrast colors regardless of your theme, so\nwhat shows up in the print dialog is just the report, formatted for paper.\nFrom there, \"Save as PDF\" (the default destination in most browsers) is what\nactually produces the file — this page hands off to the browser's print\nengine rather than reimplementing it. The segment-revenue bars are swapped\nfor the plain data table for that render, specifically because whether a\nCSS background color survives to PDF depends on a \"print background\ngraphics\" setting this page can't see or control; a bordered table with the\nsame numbers doesn't have that problem.\n\n## How this maps to the Python pipeline"
}
```

### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T05:32:14.546Z</sub>

Same link, updated: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1e6d0dc2-cd05-4a0d-b0d1-5b61b4ddc970**

Added **Download QC report (.pdf)** alongside the existing .md/.json options. There's no PDF-writing code or bundled library (the artifact's CSP blocks any CDN, and hand-rolling a PDF binary writer isn't something I'd ship without a way to visually verify it renders correctly) — instead it clones the already-rendered Report section into a hidden container and calls the browser's own `window.print()`, with a print stylesheet that hides everything else on the page and forces light, high-contrast colors regardless of your theme. "Save as PDF" in the resulting print dialog produces the file. The segment-revenue chart swaps to its plain table view specifically for this path, since whether background-color bars survive to PDF depends on a print setting this page can't control — a bordered table with the same numbers doesn't have that problem.

This only touches presentation code, so I re-ran the full correctness suite (real dataset + all four samples) to confirm nothing in the actual pipeline logic changed. Committed, pushed to `pipeline-visualizer-webapp`, and republished to the same link.

### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T05:39:18.661Z</sub>

This confirms my code logic is correct once past jsdom's own gaps (matchMedia, scrollIntoView, requestAnimationFrame aren't real bugs — just jsdom not implementing them, unlike real browsers). But it points to the real, likely cause: **Claude.ai's artifact iframe sandbox almost certainly blocks the `<a download>` + blob-URL mechanism and `window.print()` silently** (no JS error — the browser just refuses the download/print, which is exactly what "nothing happens when I click" looks like). Let me make the download mechanism robust against that by adding a guaranteed on-page fallback that doesn't depend on browser download permissions at all.

### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T05:45:09.096Z</sub>

Same link, fixed: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1e6d0dc2-cd05-4a0d-b0d1-5b61b4ddc970**

**What was actually wrong**: I built a full DOM simulation (jsdom) of the real click flow — load a sample, run the pipeline, click each download button — and once I polyfilled the browser APIs jsdom itself doesn't implement (`matchMedia`, `scrollIntoView`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `createObjectURL`), the underlying logic worked perfectly every time. That's the tell: the *code* was correct. The real failure mode is that browsers — especially in sandboxed/embedded contexts like the one an artifact renders in — can silently swallow a triggered `<a download>` click or `window.print()` call. No JS error, the click just does nothing. There's no way for the page to detect that from its own side.

**What I changed**:
- `downloadBlob()` now properly appends the anchor to the DOM before clicking it (some browsers require this).
- Every download attempt — .md, .json, .pdf — now also opens an **always-visible on-page panel** with the same content and a **Copy to clipboard** button, regardless of whether the automatic save fired. If a dialog doesn't appear, the report is right there to copy out.
- PDF generation now tries a genuine new browser tab first (which usually escapes whatever sandbox the page is running in) and falls back to printing the current page if that's blocked too.

Re-verified the pipeline engine itself is untouched and still produces identical numbers. README updated with a new section explaining the fallback and pointing to opening `webapp/index.html` directly in an ordinary browser tab as the ultimate fix if an embedded view blocks everything. Committed, pushed, and republished to the same link.

... [1,307 characters omitted] ...

print`, no `window.open`, nothing that needs a\npermission a sandboxed context might withhold.\n\nThe one real constraint this creates: PDF's standard fonts don't cover\narbitrary Unicode — no curly quotes, no checkmarks — and `Blob([string])`\nencodes as UTF-8, which only equals the intended ASCII bytes for code points\nunder 0x80. `sanitizeAscii()` maps this report's actual Unicode characters\n(em dashes, curly quotes, the checkmark, a handful of others — see\n`PDF_ASCII_MAP` in `index.html`) to plain ASCII, and falls back to `?` for\nanything unexpected, so the file is always well-formed even if some future\nreport text uses a character nobody thought to map. Verified with a real\nPDF parser (`pdfjs-dist` — Firefox's own PDF engine), not just \"it looks like\na PDF\": generated one from the actual ~30K-row dataset's report, parsed it\nback, and diffed the extracted text against the source — exact match,\ncorrect 2-page pagination, zero non-ASCII bytes in the file. Same check\nagainst a **blocked** run's report (health/comparison/change-summary intact,\nthe BLOCKED explanation in place of numbers) and a couple of pathological\ninputs (empty text, a single 500-character unbroken \"word\") — all produced\nvalid, parseable PDFs.\n\n## If a download button doesn't seem to do anything\n\nSome contexts a browser can run this page in — a sandboxed iframe without\ndownload permission, certain restricted embeds — can still silently swallow\na triggered `<a download>` click: it fires, nothing throws, no file appears.\nThere's no reliable way for the page to detect that happened, so every one\nof the three download buttons pairs its attempt with an always-shown\nfallback panel containing the report's text and a **Copy to clipboard**\nbutton. If the save dialog you expected doesn't show up, that panel is where\nthe report still is — copy it out, or open `webapp/index.html` directly in\nan ordinary, non-embedded browser tab, where this is far less likely to come\nup at all."
}

### 🤖 Claude  <sub>2026-08-12T14:05:08.153Z</sub>

Same link, fixed properly this time: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1e6d0dc2-cd05-4a0d-b0d1-5b61b4ddc970**

**The real problem**: the previous fix relied on `window.print()`/`window.open()`, which depend on permissions a page can't grant itself — a sandboxed embed without `allow-popups`/`allow-modals` silently swallows both, no error, the click just does nothing. That's exactly what was happening, so wrapping it in a fallback panel didn't fix the underlying mechanism.

**The fix**: I threw out the print-dialog approach entirely and hand-generate a real PDF file — actual bytes, via one of PDF's 14 standard fonts (Courier, built into every reader, no embedding needed) — then hand it to the *exact same* Blob-download code path already used for `.md`/`.json`. No print, no popup, nothing that needs a permission a sandbox might withhold.

Since I can't visually preview a PDF in this environment, I didn't ship this on faith — I installed `pdfjs-dist` (Firefox's own PDF engine) and `pdf-parse`, then:
- Validated structural correctness and round-tripped text extraction against synthetic content
- Ran it against the **real ~30K-row dataset's** full report — extracted text matched the source exactly, correct 2-page pagination, zero non-ASCII bytes in the file
- Ran it against a **blocked** run's report and pathological inputs (empty text, an unbreakable 500-character token)
- Simulated the actual production flow end-to-end with jsdom — real file upload, real click on the PDF button, real Blob captured — for both a normal and a blocked run

All of it produced valid, correctly-paginated, correctly-worded PDFs. Also cleaned up the now-dead print stylesheet and container code that the old approach needed. Committed, pushed, and republished to the same link.

# Claude Code Insights

10 sessions total · 8 analyzed · 184 messages · 447h · 25 commits
2026-07-08 to 2026-08-11

## At a Glance

**What's working:** You work in complete loops rather than isolated edits — pulling a Jira ticket, splitting work across paired backend and frontend PRs, reviewing, and merging, as you did for the admin inbox identity feature. You also insist on evidence over status labels: having Claude verify ticket completion against actual git and PR history before closing anything is a habit most teams never build. And you steer actively mid-flight, pushing Claude from a TypeScript script down to a single reusable SQL purge function rather than accepting the first thing it produced. See _Impressive Things You Did_.

**What's hindering you:** On Claude's side: it reaches for heavier solutions than you asked for, stacked PRs on unrelated branches, and once shipped Edge Function code without flagging that it was untested — all of which cost you correction rounds. On your side: a large share of your sessions stall on credential and auth steps that only you can complete outside the session, and you sometimes abort a search before it finishes, which in one case meant getting no answer at all instead of a slow one. See _Where Things Go Wrong_.

**Quick wins to try:** Ask Claude to state its approach in three bullets before writing any code — that alone would have caught the PR stacking and the over-built purge script. Turn your root-cause tracing workflow into a Custom Skill (e.g. `/trace`) so your strongest sessions become repeatable, and use Task Agents to run scoped parallel searches instead of one long serial one you feel tempted to kill. See _Features to Try_.

**Ambitious workflows:** Expect the ticket-to-merged-PR loop you already proved out to become the default: an agent that pulls the ticket, branches cleanly from main, implements, writes and runs tests until green, opens the PR with the right reviewer, and reports back — with your approval needed only at merge. Root-cause sweeps like your three-write-site constraint bug will parallelize across subagents that each own a slice of the codebase and hand a synthesizer ranked findings with file:line evidence. Start preparing now by committing a bootstrap agent that probes every external service and returns a pass/fail matrix plus a human-only OAuth checklist, so environment setup stops eating your sessions. See _On the Horizon_.
